name: Ellansé (PCL filler)

lead: Ellansé is an injectable filler made of tiny polycaprolactone (PCL) microspheres in a gel carrier. People use it for longer-lasting facial volume, in nasolabial folds, volume loss in the face and hands, and sometimes skin quality.

The gel carrier gives immediate volume and is absorbed, while the PCL microspheres remain and prompt the body to lay down new collagen around them as they slowly degrade. Published studies are mostly small prospective or retrospective series plus a randomized comparison between PCL products, and authors describe results lasting longer than many hyaluronic acid fillers.

paras: A licensed clinician injects it in an office visit, with volume visible at once and further firming reported as collagen builds over time. It is discussed alongside other fillers as a longer-lasting option within facial volumisation and contouring.

Reported effects include swelling and bruising and, more rarely, delayed foreign-body reactions or granulomas that have needed specialist management. Fillers are regulated as medical devices and availability varies by country.

angle.text: Ellansé is a collagen-stimulating filler used for longer-lasting facial volume. Its microspheres prompt the body to lay down new collagen around them over time, on top of the immediate volume from the gel. Support comes from small prospective studies and a randomized comparison between PCL products.

lead: Ellansé is a brand of injectable dermal filler whose active component is polycaprolactone (PCL), a biodegradable polyester, formulated as microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel carrier. It belongs to the class of collagen stimulators (biostimulators): rather than only adding volume itself, it is described as prompting the body to lay down new collagen around the microspheres.[1][2]

Published uses include correction of nasolabial folds, volume augmentation of the face and hands, and improvement of skin quality when diluted and placed in the dermis.[1][3][4] Clinical papers describe the effect as lasting longer than that of many hyaluronic acid fillers, with the microspheres degrading gradually over time.[2] Evidence consists of prospective studies, a randomized comparison between PCL products, small biopsy and case-series studies, and expert recommendations.[1][3][2][4][5]

Reported adverse effects include injection-site reactions, and rarer delayed events such as foreign-body reactions and granulomas, for which case reports and a treatment report using ultrasound guidance exist.[6][7] The product appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion mainly as a long-lasting option within facial volumisation and contouring, alongside other fillers.
infobox: About 25 to 50 micrometres (Ellansé-S, per a 2022 case series)[2]
Nasolabial folds, facial and hand volume, skin thickening

paras: Ellansé consists of PCL microspheres suspended in an aqueous carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) gel. In one retrospective series the formulation was described as roughly 30 percent PCL microspheres of 25 to 50 micrometres in a 70 percent CMC gel carrier.[2] The gel carrier provides initial volume, and is then absorbed, while the microspheres persist and are said by authors to act as a scaffold for collagen formation (neocollagenesis).[1][2]

PCL is a synthetic polyester that breaks down by hydrolysis of its ester bonds, more slowly than polylactide, a property that has made it attractive for long-term biomedical implants.[8] It was first synthesised in the early 1930s by a DuPont research group and later used in drug-delivery devices and sutures, before tissue engineering renewed interest in it.[8]

Published recommendations describe use of Ellansé for volume augmentation and rejuvenation of the face and hands, including the cheeks and other areas of volume loss.[1] A European multicenter prospective study evaluated it for nasolabial fold correction.[4] A retrospective series of nine patients examined it for long-term facial volume augmentation.[2]

A separate small prospective study placed a diluted amount of PCL filler into the dermis to examine skin-quality effects, rather than deep volume.[3] Some injectors have also described using tumescent anaesthesia techniques to reduce pain, swelling and bruising during injection.[9]

A European multicenter prospective study of 90 people with moderate to severe nasolabial folds (Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale 3 to 4) followed participants after a single treatment session to assess long-term safety and efficacy.[4] A randomized, participant- and evaluator-blinded, matched-pair study compared PCL-based fillers with one another in nasolabial fold correction.[5]

A single-clinic prospective study of 13 patients took biopsies after a single injection of 0.5 mL diluted PCL filler into the dermis, and its authors reported histological evidence of neocollagenesis and dermal thickening.[3] A retrospective case series of nine patients used objective measurement to assess the long-term volumizing action of the filler.[2] Expert consensus recommendations for face and hand use were published in 2017.[1]

Registered trials include a post-market study of Ellansé-S in nasolabial folds (NCT06984835, 126 participants, active as of the registry entry) and a 20-person study of tissue responses to biostimulatory injections (NCT06093815).[10][11] Preclinical work includes a rat-model evaluation of novel particle-free PCL fillers and a rheological comparison of porous PCL microsphere fillers.[12][13] Studies are generally small and often industry-adjacent, and head-to-head comparisons with other biostimulators are limited.

A case report described a foreign-body reaction appearing three years after injection of Ellansé.[6] A 2024 report described ultrasound-guided treatment of PCL granulomas.[7] Authors of injection-technique papers note that, as with other fillers, swelling and bruising are common after treatment, and that tumescent anaesthesia has been proposed to reduce them.[9]

Because PCL microspheres degrade slowly, nodules or granulomas can persist, and published management reports have described approaches such as ultrasound-guided treatment.[7] Vascular complications described for dermal fillers generally, including rare vision loss, are covered in the general dermal-filler literature.[14]

In the United States the FDA regulates dermal fillers as medical devices, and only a limited number are approved.[14] In the UK and EEA fillers need a CE mark, which covers manufacturing standards rather than proven efficacy.[14] Approval status for Ellansé specifically varies by market.

timeline.event: Polycaprolactone first synthesised by a DuPont research group.[8]
